lines.raw: Join every data type for each person, then find who has which condition.

lines.raw: In this lesson you will:
lines.say: In this lesson you will:

lines.raw: Name the data types a population health team combines, and what each adds.
lines.say: Name the data types a population health team combines, and what each adds.

lines.raw: Explain why the population must start from eligibility.
lines.say: Explain why the population must start from eligibility.

lines.raw: Read a simple condition identification rule and apply it to members.
lines.say: Read a simple condition identification rule and apply it to members.

lines.raw: One person, many data sources.
lines.say: One person, many data sources.

lines.raw: No single data type tells the whole story.
lines.say: No single data type tells the whole story.

lines.raw: A pharmacy claim shows Robert takes metformin, but not his blood sugar.
lines.say: A pharmacy claim shows Robert takes metformin, but not his blood sugar.

lines.raw: A lab result shows his sugar, but not whether he went to hospital.
lines.say: A lab result shows his sugar, but not whether he went to hospital.

lines.raw: So the team **joins all the data types for each person**, using the **member ID** as the key.
lines.say: So the team joins all the data types for each person, using the member I D as the key.

lines.raw: Like a family file at the health post.
lines.say: Like a family file at the health post.

lines.raw: Imagine one folder per household at a health post: the vaccination card, the OPD tickets, the lab reports, the weight chart and the FCHV's notes, all clipped together.
lines.say: Imagine one folder per household at a health post: the vaccination card, the O P D tickets, the lab reports, the weight chart and the FCHV's notes, all clipped together.

lines.raw: Nobody could see the full picture from one sheet.
lines.say: Nobody could see the full picture from one sheet.

lines.raw: Population health builds that folder for every member, from data.
lines.say: Population health builds that folder for every member, from data.

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: **Eligibility**. What it adds: Who is in the population, and for which months. The **denominator**: everyone counts, even people with no claims. Example for Robert (2025): Covered all 12 months of 2025 on his Medicare Advantage plan.
lines.say: Eligibility. What it adds: Who is in the population, and for which months. The denominator: everyone counts, even people with no claims. Example for Robert (2025): Covered all 12 months of 2025 on his Medicare Advantage plan.

lines.raw: **Medical claims**. What it adds: Diagnoses (as **ICD-10** codes, from the International Classification of Diseases; see the Medical course), visits, hospital stays, emergency room (ER) visits, procedures. Example for Robert (2025): Doctor visits on 14 Mar and 12 Sep with `E11.9` (type 2 diabetes) and `I10` (high blood pressure); one ER visit for dizziness.
lines.say: Medical claims. What it adds: Diagnoses (as I C D 10 codes, from the International Classification of Diseases; see the Medical course), visits, hospital stays, emergency room (E R) visits, procedures. Example for Robert (2025): Doctor visits on 14 Mar and 12 Sep with E 1 1 . 9 (type 2 diabetes) and I10 (high blood pressure); one E R visit for dizziness.

lines.raw: **Pharmacy claims**. What it adds: Which medicines, and whether they are refilled on time. Example for Robert (2025): Metformin and lisinopril (a blood pressure medicine) filled every month.
lines.say: Pharmacy claims. What it adds: Which medicines, and whether they are refilled on time. Example for Robert (2025): Metformin and lisinopril (a blood pressure medicine) filled every month.

lines.raw: **Lab results**. What it adds: Test values: how well a condition is controlled. For diabetes the key test is the **A1c**, which shows average blood sugar over about the last 3 months. Example for Robert (2025): A1c 8.4% on 12 Sep 2025.
lines.say: Lab results. What it adds: Test values: how well a condition is controlled. For diabetes the key test is the A1c, which shows average blood sugar over about the last 3 months. Example for Robert (2025): A1c 8.4 percent on 12 Sep 2025.

lines.raw: **Biometrics**. What it adds: Height, weight, blood pressure, BMI (body mass index: weight compared with height). Example for Robert (2025): Blood pressure 148/92 at his September visit.
lines.say: Biometrics. What it adds: Height, weight, blood pressure, B M I (body mass index: weight compared with height). Example for Robert (2025): Blood pressure 148/92 at his September visit.

lines.raw: **Other**. What it adds: Health surveys, care manager notes, social needs such as no transport or no job (lesson 5). Example for Robert (2025): Survey: drives himself, no social needs reported.
lines.say: Other. What it adds: Health surveys, care manager notes, social needs such as no transport or no job (lesson 5). Example for Robert (2025): Survey: drives himself, no social needs reported.

lines.raw: People with no claims still count.
lines.say: People with no claims still count.

lines.raw: A member who never went to a doctor has **no** medical or pharmacy rows.
lines.say: A member who never went to a doctor has no medical or pharmacy rows.

lines.raw: If you build your population from claims only, they disappear.
lines.say: If you build your population from claims only, they disappear.

lines.raw: Always start from **eligibility**, then attach claims.
lines.say: Always start from eligibility, then attach claims.

lines.raw: Someone with no claims in two years may be healthy, or may be avoiding care, and both are worth knowing.
lines.say: Someone with no claims in two years may be healthy, or may be avoiding care, and both are worth knowing.

lines.raw: Claims arrive late.
lines.say: Claims arrive late.

lines.raw: Doctors and hospitals can send claims weeks or months after the visit.
lines.say: Doctors and hospitals can send claims weeks or months after the visit.

lines.raw: So a report run on 1 January will be missing some December care.
lines.say: So a report run on 1 January will be missing some December care.

lines.raw: Teams usually wait for most claims to arrive (often a few months) before trusting a full year's numbers.
lines.say: Teams usually wait for most claims to arrive (often a few months) before trusting a full year's numbers.

lines.raw: This waiting time is called **claims run-out** or **lag**.
lines.say: This waiting time is called claims run-out or lag.

lines.raw: Finding who has which condition.
lines.say: Finding who has which condition.

lines.raw: Before you can build a diabetes registry, you need to decide **who has diabetes**.
lines.say: Before you can build a diabetes registry, you need to decide who has diabetes.

lines.raw: There is no "has diabetes = yes" column.
lines.say: There is no "has diabetes = yes" column.

lines.raw: Instead, analysts write a **condition identification rule** that looks for evidence in the data.
lines.say: Instead, analysts write a condition identification rule that looks for evidence in the data.

lines.raw: Why not just "any claim with a diabetes code"?
lines.say: Why not just "any claim with a diabetes code"?

lines.raw: Because codes are sometimes used when a doctor is only **checking** for a condition, or a code is entered by mistake.
lines.say: Because codes are sometimes used when a doctor is only checking for a condition, or a code is entered by mistake.

lines.raw: Requiring more than one piece of evidence makes the list more reliable.
lines.say: Requiring more than one piece of evidence makes the list more reliable.

lines.raw: An example diabetes rule (a common style, simplified).
lines.say: An example diabetes rule (a common style, simplified).

lines.raw: 2+ outpatient claims ... on different dates: Two separate doctor visits both recorded diabetes, so it is unlikely to be a one-off mistake.
lines.say: 2+ outpatient claims ... on different dates: Two separate doctor visits both recorded diabetes, so it is unlikely to be a one-off mistake.

lines.raw: E10.x or E11.x: ICD-10 codes for type 1 (`E10`) and type 2 (`E11`) diabetes, with any extra digits.
lines.say: E 1 0 . x or E 1 1 . x: I C D 10 codes for type 1 (E10) and type 2 (E11) diabetes, with any extra digits.

lines.raw: 1+ inpatient claim: A hospital stay where diabetes was coded.
lines.say: 1+ inpatient claim: A hospital stay where diabetes was coded.

lines.raw: One is enough because hospital coding is detailed.
lines.say: One is enough because hospital coding is detailed.

lines.raw: 1+ fill of a diabetes medicine: Pharmacy evidence, for example insulin.
lines.say: 1+ fill of a diabetes medicine: Pharmacy evidence, for example insulin.

lines.raw: Real rules are careful here: metformin is sometimes prescribed for other reasons, so some rules need a diagnosis too.
lines.say: Real rules are careful here: metformin is sometimes prescribed for other reasons, so some rules need a diagnosis too.

lines.raw: Where do real rules come from?
lines.say: Where do real rules come from?

lines.raw: Many teams borrow rules from published standards, such as the definitions used in HEDIS quality measures, or from their analytics vendor.
lines.say: Many teams borrow rules from published standards, such as the definitions used in HEDIS quality measures, or from their analytics vendor.

lines.raw: The exact counts and look-back periods (often 1 or 2 years) vary.
lines.say: The exact counts and look-back periods (often 1 or 2 years) vary.

lines.raw: Always write down which rule you used.
lines.say: Always write down which rule you used.

lines.raw: Applying rules to our members (2024 to 2025 look-back).
lines.say: Applying rules to our members (2024 to 2025 look-back).

lines.raw: Robert. Evidence found: 2 outpatient claims with `E11.9` on different dates + monthly metformin fills + A1c 8.4%. Condition flagged: **Diabetes** ✅ and **high blood pressure** ✅ (`I10` on 2 visits + lisinopril).
lines.say: Robert. Evidence found: 2 outpatient claims with E 1 1 . 9 on different dates and monthly metformin fills and A1c 8.4 percent. Condition flagged: Diabetes ✅ and high blood pressure ✅ (I10 on 2 visits and lisinopril).

lines.raw: Emily. Evidence found: July 2025 check-up with `E78.5` (high cholesterol) + atorvastatin fills from 15 Jul 2025. Condition flagged: **High cholesterol** ✅.
lines.say: Emily. Evidence found: July 2025 check-up with E 7 8 . 5 (high cholesterol) and atorvastatin fills from 15 Jul 2025. Condition flagged: High cholesterol ✅.

lines.say: Emily. Evidence found: Appendix stay, 2 to 4 Jun 2025, K 3 5 . 8 0. Condition flagged: Not a chronic condition. Recorded as a past hospital stay, not a flag.

lines.say: Daniel. Evidence found: One check-up in August 2025, no chronic codes. Condition flagged: None (his doctor did record that he had lost his job, a social need covered in lesson 5).

lines.say: Lily. Evidence found: Well-child check-up and routine vaccines, no chronic codes. Condition flagged: None.

lines.say: In the U S: What a population health dataset looks like.

lines.raw: Usually **one row per member per month** (or per year), built from eligibility.
lines.say: Usually one row per member per month (or per year), built from eligibility.

lines.say: Columns are added from every source: member_months, has_diabetes, l a s t _ a 1 c, i p _ s t a y s _ 1 2 m, e r _ v i s i t s _ 1 2 m, allowed_amt.

lines.raw: Three checks catch most problems: **every eligible member has a row** (even with no claims), **every flag says which rule and look-back it used**, and **`NULL` means "no data", not "normal"**: Emily has no A1c because she was never tested, not because her sugar is fine.
lines.say: Three checks catch most problems: every eligible member has a row (even with no claims), every flag says which rule and look-back it used, and N U L L means "no data", not "normal": Emily has no A1c because she was never tested, not because her sugar is fine.
